title: Java Optional
learningObjectives: Represent a possibly absent return value with Optional<T>
Create present and empty Optional values using standard factories
Transform present values with map and filter operations
Provide lazy fallback values using orElseGet when appropriate
Avoid unsafe get calls when an Optional may be empty

understand.concept: Optional represents a value that may be absent and is most useful as a method return type. Use map and filter, and orElseGet for lazy fallback calculation.
understand.whyItMatters: Java Optional helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Representing optional results

Optional<T> is a container that either holds one non-null value or is empty. It is commonly used as a method return type when a result may legitimately be absent. It makes absence explicit in the API rather than relying on an undocumented null convention.

## Creating Optional values

Optional.of(value) requires a non-null value and throws NullPointerException for null. Optional.ofNullable(value) creates an empty Optional when its argument is null. Optional.empty() creates an empty instance. Do not use Optional as a replacement for every nullable field or as a parameter type by default; follow the API design conventions of the surrounding codebase.

## Transforming and filtering

map applies a function when a value is present and wraps the mapped result. If the Optional is empty, map returns an empty Optional without calling the function. filter keeps the value only when the predicate is true. flatMap is useful when the mapping function already returns Optional and avoids nested Optional<Optional<T>> values.

## Supplying fallback values

orElse(value) evaluates its argument before the call, even when the Optional is present. orElseGet(supplier) evaluates the supplier only when the Optional is empty, making it preferable when computing the fallback is expensive or has side effects. orElseThrow can provide an exception when a required value is absent.

## Safe inspection

Use isPresent/isEmpty when a branch is needed, ifPresent for an action on a present value, and map/filter/orElseGet for value-oriented pipelines. Avoid calling get without first establishing presence; it throws NoSuchElementException when empty.

## API design

Optional is primarily intended for return values. It does not make the underlying lookup successful or validate business rules. Decide what absence means and document the fallback or error policy.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<String> value = java.util.Optional.of("Java"); System.out.println(value.orElse("none")); } }
examples.explanation: Optional.of stores a non-null value, and orElse returns that value because it is present.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<String> value = java.util.Optional.empty(); System.out.println(value.orElse("fallback")); } }
examples.explanation: Optional.empty represents absence; orElse supplies a fallback without changing the Optional itself.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<String> value = java.util.Optional.of("java"); System.out.println(value.map(String::toUpperCase).orElse("none")); } }
examples.explanation: map applies the transformation only when the Optional contains a value and wraps the transformed result.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<Integer> value = java.util.Optional.of(5); System.out.println(value.filter(n -> n > 3).isPresent()); } }
examples.explanation: filter retains a present value only when the predicate is true; otherwise the result is empty.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.Optional<String> value = java.util.Optional.ofNullable(null); System.out.println(value.isEmpty()); } }
examples.explanation: ofNullable converts a possibly null reference into a present or empty Optional without throwing for null.

practise.guidedTask: Write a method that returns Optional<String> for a lookup that may fail. Use map, filter and orElseGet without calling get().
practise.independentTask: Build a configuration lookup that returns Optional values and supplies a lazy default only when a key is missing.
hints: Use of only when the value is known to be non-null; use ofNullable when null is a possible input.
map transforms a present value, filter tests it, and flatMap avoids nested Optional values.
Use orElseGet for a lazily computed fallback; avoid get unless presence is already guaranteed.
practise.challenge: Test Optional.of, ofNullable(null), empty, map on empty, filter rejection and orElseGet; explain why Optional is usually best as a return type.
